Foundations

Payoff shape, survival, and the vocabulary of the thesis.

Part 1 · 15 terms

  1. A payoff where the upside and downside are unequal in size or probability. The framework seeks it deliberately and treats symmetric risk measures as an incomplete description of survival.

    Part 1 · Shape the payoff Exhibit S1 · Shape the Payoff

    Related Convexity Barbell Fragility

  2. Missing a thesis break because there is more information than attention. The framework answers it with tripwires, which automate attention to the critical signals so a break is noticed when it happens rather than when it becomes convenient.

    Part 1 · The failure modes the system answers Exhibit L3 · Govern the Thesis

    Related Tripwire Agentic verification Intra-week triggers

  3. A structure that pairs very safe holdings with a small, highly convex allocation and skips the fragile middle. It targets payoff asymmetry, not low volatility.

    Part 5 · Portfolio construction and posture expression

    Related Convexity Fragility Ballast Torque

  4. Exposure where the upside can compound far faster than the downside, so being right pays off disproportionately more than being wrong costs.

    Part 5 · How convexity is expressed through Posture Exhibit S1 · Shape the Payoff

    Related CIS Posture Torque Fragility Power-law corridor

  5. A decline from a position’s or portfolio’s recent peak. The framework treats a survivable drawdown as the price of convexity rather than as a malfunction, provided reserves make it holdable.

    Part 5 · Drawdown tolerance Exhibit P5-01 · Three Jobs. One Cycle.

    Related Ballast Sequence-of-returns risk Survivability Volatility

  6. Vulnerability to disorder and nonlinear shocks, not just price movement. A fragile position breaks when stress rises.

    Part 6 · Fragility inside the CIS score Exhibit 01 · The Hedge Broke

    Related Convexity Tripwire CIS Sequence-of-returns risk

  7. Holding a deteriorating position because the story still sounds right. The framework names it as a failure mode of traditional portfolio management and answers it with quantified reassessment, so evidence rather than narrative decides whether a position stays.

    Part 1 · The failure modes the system answers

    Related CIS Thesis drift Conviction Decision log

  8. Holding a position whose future paths include large upside without committing to which one occurs. It is the property CIS scores first, because it is what convexity is made of.

    Part 6 · Convexity and Optionality inside CIS Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related Convexity Right-tail outcomes CIS

  9. Rare but very large gains that dominate total portfolio outcomes, which is why their tax treatment matters so much.

    Part 4 · Taxing the right tail Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Convexity Tax wrapper Buy, borrow, die

  10. The chance of a loss large enough to end compounding, which no later gain can repair. The framework treats ruin as a boundary condition rather than a risk to be traded off: survival comes first, because nothing compounds from zero.

    Part 2 · Taleb: antifragility and ruin avoidance Exhibit P2-02 · Ruin Comes First

    Related Fragility Survivable compounding Sequence-of-returns risk Barbell

  11. The risk that the order of gains and losses, not just their average, determines whether a portfolio survives. A large drawdown at the wrong time can permanently impair compounding.

    Part 5 · Position sizing against sequence risk Exhibit 05 · Path Changes Everything

    Related Survivable compounding Fragility Posture

  12. Whether a position or portfolio can withstand stress without being forced into a decision that ends the compounding. It is scored inside CIS as Risk and Fragility, where a higher score means lower fragility.

    Part 6 · Risk and Fragility inside CIS Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related Fragility Drawdown CIS Ballast

  13. Building a portfolio that can stay alive through timing errors, volatility, and thesis delays while keeping exposure to large upside.

    Part 1 · Survivable compounding under uncertainty Exhibit 06 · Survive the Path

    Related Convexity Fragility Posture Sequence-of-returns risk

  14. How much a price moves. The framework separates it from fragility: a position can be highly volatile and still robust, and the difference is whether the move threatens survival.

    Part 1 · Fragility is not volatility Exhibit P3-03 · Volatility Is the Toll

    Related Fragility Drawdown Survivability

  15. High-volatility periods tend to arrive in clusters rather than as isolated events, which changes how risk should be managed.

    Part 1 · The traditional playbook is failing quietly

    Related Fragility Momentum filter

Lineage & Macro

Regime, thesis, and the policy backdrop.

Part 2 · 7 terms

  1. Correlations between assets are regime-dependent and can flip when inflation or liquidity stress dominates.

    Part 2 · Why the diversification regime changed Exhibit 02 · Correlation Turns

    Related Macro thesis Fragility

  2. A condition where public debt and financing constraints begin to dictate what monetary policy can realistically do.

    Part 2 · The macro thesis and policy backdrop Exhibit 04 · The Bill Came Due

    Related Macro thesis Policy reflexivity

  3. The aggregate supply of money and credit in the system, read through measures such as M2 growth, central-bank balance sheets, and real rates. The framework treats its expansion and contraction as a tide that convex assets amplify rather than merely follow.

    Part 2 · Lyn Alden: liquidity cycles Exhibit P2-09 · Liquidity Sets the Tide

    Related Macro thesis Fiscal dominance Regime Policy reflexivity

  4. A probabilistic read of the current regime that sets the portfolio’s structure. It is a framing device, not a point forecast.

    Part 2 · The lineage and the full regime thesis Exhibit L2 · Capital Has Weather

    Related Fiscal dominance Policy reflexivity Posture Tripwire TAM

  5. Markets react to policy and policymakers react back to markets, creating feedback loops that can amplify instability.

    Part 2 · The intellectual lineage Exhibit P2-04 · Markets Feed Back

    Related Macro thesis Fiscal dominance

  6. The prevailing structural conditions that determine how assets behave and correlate. The framework is built to adapt when the regime changes rather than to optimize for the average of all regimes.

    Part 2 · Identifying the macro thesis Exhibit P2-08 · Phase Changes Sizing

    Related Macro thesis Correlation instability Regime force

  7. A durable structural driver that capital must flow toward, identified in the macro thesis. The framework allocates by force rather than by sector, and diversifies across several expressions of the same force.

    Part 5 · Allocate by force, not by sector Exhibit P5-07 · One Regime Force. Multiple Economic Expressions.

    Related Macro thesis Torque

The Backbone

Bitcoin, valuation, and accumulation.

Part 3 · 10 terms

  1. The handling rule for the backbone: Bitcoin is accumulated and never sold, traded, or rebalanced. Valuation models shape the pace of buying, not entries and exits, and cash needs are met from income, other assets, or borrowing against the reserve.

    Part 3 · Handling doctrine: accumulate, then borrow Exhibit P3-06 · Accumulate, Don’t Trade

    Related Bitcoin backbone Dollar-cost averaging Model convergence Cold storage

  2. The reserve asset and principal source of convexity: a Bitcoin position held outside the three postures, accumulated on a schedule, governed by valuation discipline, and never sold, traded, or rebalanced. Liquidity comes from elsewhere.

    Part 3 · Bitcoin as the convexity backbone Exhibit P3-03 · Volatility Is the Toll

    Related Posture Power-law corridor Dollar-cost averaging Cold storage Accumulate-only doctrine Reserve share

  3. Holding the Bitcoin reserve in hardware wallets under the holder’s own keys, accumulated through payroll contributions and held rather than trimmed on valuation. A custodian enters only if and when collateralized borrowing begins.

    Part 3 · Cold-storage architecture and the borrow phase Exhibit P3-07 · Cold Storage to Borrow

    Related Bitcoin backbone Buy, borrow, die Taxable account Accumulate-only doctrine

  4. Buying a fixed amount on a set schedule regardless of price, which spreads entry risk across time. The framework funds it from income and accelerates it into deep drawdowns.

    Part 5 · Accumulation discipline and position management Exhibit P3-06 · Accumulate, Don’t Trade

    Related Survivable compounding Ballast Sequence-of-returns risk

  5. A stretch in which Bitcoin trades well above its power-law trend and its realized-price basis. The response is to slow discretionary accumulation and build dry powder from income; an extension never prompts a sale of the reserve.

    Part 3 · Through two cycles: extension and convergence Exhibit P3-01 · Power Law Holds

    Related Model convergence Power-law corridor Dry powder Dollar-cost averaging

  6. The valuation read for Bitcoin: several independent models are compared, and their agreement is the signal. Convergence on undervaluation accelerates accumulation, convergence on overvaluation slows it, and wide divergence counsels holding the range.

    Part 3 · Power-law bands and model convergence Exhibit P3-05 · Models Must Converge

    Related Power-law corridor Realized price Dollar-cost averaging Dry powder Extension

  7. A long-run regression channel, on a log scale, that Bitcoin’s price has historically tracked. The framework reads it as a context band for accumulation pace, not a deterministic price prediction.

    Part 3 · Power-law bands and model convergence Exhibit P3-01 · Power Law Holds

    Related Convexity CIS Macro thesis

  8. Bitcoin’s aggregate on-chain cost basis, with each coin valued at the price it last moved. It rises with adoption and marks a historically important bear-market regime level, not a hard floor: price can trade below it for extended stretches.

    Part 3 · Valuation models: realized price Exhibit P3-05 · Models Must Converge

    Related Model convergence Power-law corridor Cost basis

  9. Bitcoin’s share of the whole portfolio. A ten to fifteen percent target suits long horizons and moderate risk capacity, twenty to thirty percent suits higher conviction, and a mature thirty to fifty percent share can emerge over decades through accumulation rather than rebalancing.

    Part 3 · Reserve sizing by horizon and risk capacity Exhibit P3-08 · Reserve Share Evolves

    Related Bitcoin backbone Position sizing Concentration limit Cold storage

  10. Total Addressable Market: a deliberately conservative estimate of the capital a market could absorb over time, used to size an asset’s potential rather than to forecast a price.

    Part 3 · The conservative addressable-market estimate for the Bitcoin reserve

    Related Convexity CIS Macro thesis

Tax Architecture

Wrappers, basis, and what you keep.

Part 4 · 19 terms

  1. Reaching Roth treatment above the direct income limits by contributing to a traditional IRA and converting. It preserves access under current law and is subject to the pro-rata rule when other pre-tax balances exist.

    Part 4 · Roth allocation discipline

    Related Roth account Tax wrapper

  2. Taking a deduction at a high marginal rate in one year and converting the balance to Roth in a later, lower-rate year. The captured value is the spread between the two rates.

    Part 4 · Pre-tax accounts: inferior, occasionally useful

    Related Pre-tax account Roth account

  3. Borrowing against appreciated assets instead of selling them, potentially deferring realization. It depends on current law and financing availability.

    Part 4 · Realization deferral mechanics Exhibit P3-07 · Cold Storage to Borrow

    Related Tax wrapper Right-tail outcomes

  4. The taxable profit realized when an appreciated position is sold. Long-held positions generally receive preferential rates, which is why holding period and wrapper placement change what a gain is worth.

    Part 4 · The tax wedge Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Taxable account Tax-loss harvesting Cost basis

  5. What a position is treated as having cost for tax purposes. Gains are measured against it, return-of-capital distributions reduce it, and under current law it may reset at death.

    Part 4 · Return of capital and basis

    Related Capital gains Return of capital Step-up in basis

  6. Borrowing against portfolio assets rather than selling them. The framework treats it as an optional overlay, revocable by the broker and repriceable under stress, never as a structural requirement.

    Part 4 · Margin as an optional overlay

    Related Buy, borrow, die Taxable account

  7. An additional 3.8 percent federal tax on investment income above certain income thresholds. It is part of why a taxable account retains materially less of a large gain than a Roth.

    Part 4 · The tax wedge Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Taxable account Capital gains Tax wrapper

  8. An account funded before tax where contributions reduce current income and withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. The framework treats it as tactical rather than structural, because the deferred tax obligation compounds alongside the balance.

    Part 4 · Pre-tax accounts: inferior, occasionally useful Exhibit P4-02 · Gross Is Not Net

    Related Tax wrapper Required minimum distribution Bracket arbitrage

  9. The only options use permitted inside a Roth: long calls, long puts, and defined-risk spreads, never undefined-risk strategies such as naked options or short volatility. A tactical overlay for a high-conviction thesis, capped at three to five percent of the account measured as maximum loss at entry.

    Part 4 · Options within the Roth: purchased convexity only

    Related Roth account Optionality Asymmetry Conviction

  10. A withdrawal the law compels from pre-tax accounts starting at age 73, rising to 75 in 2033 under current rules. It forces taxable income regardless of need, which is one reason the framework prefers Roth for long-horizon convexity.

    Part 4 · Pre-tax accounts: inferior, occasionally useful

    Related Pre-tax account Tax wrapper

  11. A distribution treated as a return of your own invested capital rather than taxable income. It reduces cost basis and defers tax rather than eliminating it; classification can change and depends on current law.

    Part 5 · The Ballast posture Exhibit P4-03 · ROC Changes the Yield

    Related Tax wrapper Ballast

  12. An account funded with after-tax dollars where qualified withdrawals are not taxed, so appreciation compounds and trades without tax friction. The framework treats its annual capacity as scarce and reserves it for positions that may be rotated.

    Part 4 · Reserving Roth for Torque Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Tax wrapper Torque Right-tail outcomes Backdoor Roth

  13. The reset of an inherited asset’s cost basis to its value at death under current law, which can erase the embedded gain. It is policy-dependent and not guaranteed, and it underpins the never-sell treatment of the Bitcoin backbone.

    Part 4 · Why Bitcoin sits in taxable

    Related Cost basis Buy, borrow, die Taxable account

  14. The gap between a gross gain and what a given wrapper lets you keep after tax. It widens as the outcome grows, which is why the largest wins are the ones where wrapper placement matters most.

    Part 4 · The tax wedge Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Tax wrapper Roth account Taxable account Right-tail outcomes Net investment income tax

  15. The legal account container (Roth, taxable, or pre-tax) whose tax rules materially change long-run compounding outcomes.

    Part 4 · Wrapper engineering as structural edge Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Buy, borrow, die Right-tail outcomes Survivable compounding

  16. Realizing a loss deliberately to offset gains, or a limited amount of ordinary income, while keeping the exposure through a non-identical position. The harvested loss carries forward as a durable tax asset.

    Part 4 · Tax-loss harvesting

    Related Taxable account Capital gains Wash sale

  17. An ordinary investment account with no contribution limit, where realized gains and distributions are taxed in the year they occur. The framework routes never-sold and income-producing holdings here, including the Bitcoin backbone.

    Part 4 · The work taxable accounts do Exhibit P4-03 · ROC Changes the Yield

    Related Tax wrapper Buy, borrow, die Ballast Step-up in basis

  18. What the portfolio is actually worth at the end of the horizon, after every tax, fee, and friction has been paid. The framework optimizes for it rather than for any single year’s return.

    Part 4 · Wrapper engineering as a structural edge Exhibit P4-01 · The Tax Wedge

    Related Tax wrapper Survivable compounding Right-tail outcomes

  19. A rule that disallows a realized loss when a substantially identical position is repurchased inside a set window. It is why harvesting redeploys into a similar but not identical holding.

    Part 4 · Tax-loss harvesting

    Related Tax-loss harvesting Capital gains

Construction & Governance

Postures, sizing, and the rules of change.

Part 5 · 31 terms

  1. The highest price of the past year, used as the reference for absolute momentum. Distance below it grades a position from healthy, through correction, to severe distress.

    Part 5 · Momentum: conviction requires confirmation Exhibit P5-06 · Conviction Requires Market Confirmation

    Related Momentum filter Breadth

  2. An AI-assisted research loop that speeds evidence-gathering once a tripwire fires, without handing final judgment to the machine.

    Part 5 · Verification inside position management

    Related Tripwire CIS

  3. The target size range a score maps into for a given posture. Seventy and above supports core sizing, sixty to sixty-nine constrained, fifty to fifty-nine starter, and below fifty is not allocation-worthy.

    Part 5 · The sizing tables Exhibit P5-03 · The Same Score Does Not Create the Same Position

    Related Position sizing Score band CIS Posture

  4. Capital-preserving reserve and rotation capital that helps the portfolio survive stress and buy into dislocations.

    Part 5 · The Ballast posture Exhibit P5-04 · Ballast Preserves the Right to Buy

    Related Torque Hype Posture

  5. A checklist, not an impression: a Ballast candidate must pass at least three of five tests covering a fortress balance sheet, diversified revenue, durable cash generation, low factor correlation, and a liquidity-resilient valuation. Yield is deliberately not on the list; income follows quality rather than qualifying it.

    Part 5 · Ballast: five tests, three required Exhibit P5-04 · Ballast Preserves the Right to Buy

    Related Ballast Survivability Rotation

  6. How widely a move is shared across related names. Broad participation supports a thesis; narrowing leadership warns that a move is thinning even while the index holds.

    Part 5 · Momentum: conviction requires confirmation Exhibit P5-06 · Conviction Requires Market Confirmation

    Related Momentum filter 52-week high

  7. The framework’s closed structure classification for a position: Long Carry, Short Carry, or Barbell. In CIS scoring, carry direction measures whether a position benefits from or suffers under the current rate and inflation regime; a barbell pairs the two exposures.

    Part 6 · Carry direction inside the CIS macro component

    Related Barbell Posture Convexity CIS

  8. The rule that every change to the rules is itself governed, by routing it to exactly one of three levels: doctrine, which cannot change without abandoning the framework; parameters, tunable within documented ranges; and overrides, temporary, documented, and time-bounded.

    Part 5 · Doctrine, parameters, overrides Exhibit P5-10 · Know What You Are Changing

    Related Doctrine Parameter Override Decision log

  9. A ceiling on how much any single name or small group may represent, applied to the household aggregate across every account. Fifteen percent is the default single-position cap, eighteen percent the absolute with a documented override.

    Part 5 · Concentration limits Exhibit P5-03 · The Same Score Does Not Create the Same Position

    Related Position sizing Override FIS

  10. The strength of the evidence behind a position, as opposed to enthusiasm for it. The framework quantifies it through CIS so that size follows demonstrated evidence rather than feeling.

    Part 5 · Earned size Exhibit P5-02 · Position Size Must Be Earned

    Related CIS Position sizing Allocation band

  11. The one to three claims a position depends on, written down at entry in a form that can be checked. They are what thesis drift is measured against: when one breaks, the position is reassessed on the evidence, whatever the price is doing.

    Part 5 · Protocol 05: one to three core assertions per position

    Related Thesis drift Decision log Conviction CIS

  12. The non-negotiable layer of the framework: the principles that define what it is. Changing one means no longer implementing the framework, as distinct from tuning a parameter or logging an override.

    Part 5 · Doctrine, parameters, overrides Exhibit P5-10 · Know What You Are Changing

    Related Override Posture

  13. Reserve cash kept ready to deploy into dislocations. The framework builds it during extensions and spends it when valuations converge on undervaluation.

    Part 5 · Reserve capital and redeployment rules

    Related Ballast Posture Sequence-of-returns risk

  14. The protocol governing exposure around a scheduled earnings date. A position entering the final five trading days is capped at three percent of portfolio value, because the event is binary and conviction does not predict it.

    Part 5 · Earnings proximity: cap the binary event Exhibit P5-05 · Conviction Does Not Eliminate Binary Risk

    Related Tripwire Position sizing

  15. The portfolio boundary for every concentration rule: the total across all wrappers, including Roth, pre-tax, taxable, and Bitcoin cold storage. A position held in several accounts sums to one exposure, and the limits apply to that sum rather than to any single account.

    Part 5 · The portfolio boundary and single-name sleeves

    Related Concentration limit Single-name sleeve Tax wrapper Position sizing

  16. Narrative-driven convexity with weak structural backing. Useful only with strict limits and automatic exits.

    Part 5 · The Hype posture and its limits Exhibit P5-03 · The Same Score Does Not Create the Same Position

    Related Torque Ballast Posture Convexity

  17. A trend-validation rule: the framework checks that the market is confirming the thesis before it allows a full position size.

    Part 5 · Momentum as the sizing gate Exhibit P5-06 · Conviction Requires Market Confirmation

    Related Tripwire CIS Macro thesis

  18. A conscious, documented, time-bounded deviation from a default parameter, carrying the reasoning and the conditions under which it reverts. An unexamined drift is not an override; it is the framework being abandoned quietly.

    Part 5 · Doctrine, parameters, overrides Exhibit P5-10 · Know What You Are Changing

    Related Doctrine Concentration limit

  19. The middle layer of change governance: a threshold that may be tuned inside a documented envelope for an articulated reason, such as component weights, sizing bands, momentum thresholds, or concentration limits. Changing one adjusts the framework; changing doctrine abandons it.

    Part 5 · Doctrine, parameters, overrides Exhibit P5-10 · Know What You Are Changing

    Related Doctrine Override Change governance Delta clamp

  20. A rule on the way in: a position down twenty percent or more from cost basis takes no new capital until a confirming signal arrives, such as a higher low, a reclaimed level, or new thesis-supporting evidence. Scaling in happens over weeks, with no more than a quarter of the target added in any one week.

    Part 5 · Adds and freezes: discipline on the way in

    Related Position sizing Momentum filter Drawdown Conviction

  21. How much capital a single position is allowed to carry. In this framework size is earned: the score selects a band, the posture scales it, and concentration limits cap it at the household level.

    Part 5 · Sizing by posture Exhibit P5-03 · The Same Score Does Not Create the Same Position

    Related Allocation band Concentration limit Posture CIS

  22. The behavioral classification every non-Bitcoin position carries: Torque, Ballast, or Hype. It sets the position’s sizing bands and governance rules; behavior, not asset type, is what the framework classifies. Bitcoin sits outside all three, governed by Part 3.

    Part 5 · The three postures in full Exhibit P5-01 · Three Jobs. One Cycle.

    Related Torque Ballast Hype Macro thesis

  23. The Hype exit schedule: one third of the position is sold at a fifty percent gain, another third at one hundred percent, and the remainder runs with the stop raised to breakeven. It converts a narrative trade into banked gains without pretending to know the top.

    Part 5 · Hype governance Exhibit P5-03 · The Same Score Does Not Create the Same Position

    Related Hype Stop-loss Rotation

  24. A state machine for stressed markets, when rising correlation and departing liquidity make positions that looked independent trade as one. The response is deliberately boring: pause new Torque adds, enforce posture limits strictly, consider trimming gross exposure by ten to twenty percent, and resume only after two calm weeks.

    Part 5 · Liquidity and correlation: throttle the regime Exhibit P5-09 · When Correlation Rises, Diversification Shrinks

    Related Correlation instability Correlation stacking Torque Tripwire

  25. Moving capital between postures as conditions change, most often trimming Ballast after Torque runs and redeploying into Torque during dislocations. It is the framework’s primary way of buying low without raising outside cash.

    Part 5 · The rotation function Exhibit P5-04 · Ballast Preserves the Right to Buy

    Related Ballast Torque Dry powder

  26. A wrapper intentionally concentrated in one position, permitted only while the household aggregate stays inside its limits. The designation is explicit and documented, drift is monitored, and trimming is required if the aggregate breaches a cap. A governance structure, not an exception.

    Part 5 · The portfolio boundary and single-name sleeves

    Related Household aggregate Concentration limit Roth account Override

  27. An exit level committed to before entry. Hype positions carry them by doctrine, and the framework forbids widening a stop or reclassifying a position to avoid honoring one.

    Part 5 · Hype governance

    Related Hype Tripwire

  28. The truth problem, as distinct from the price problem: a core assertion behind a position has broken. Reassessment is immediate and price is irrelevant; a thesis-damaged position is downgraded or exited, and a later price recovery does not rehabilitate it.

    Part 5 · Thesis drift: price problems versus truth problems

    Related Core assertions Momentum filter Tripwire Narrative drift

  29. Controlled convexity: high-upside exposure to durable, real regime forces that can tolerate serious drawdowns.

    Part 5 · The Torque posture Exhibit P5-01 · Three Jobs. One Cycle.

    Related Ballast Hype Posture Convexity

  30. The gate a position must pass before it can be Torque, and entry is earned three ways at once: a structural tailwind from an identifiable regime force, business survivability through stress without continuous access to capital markets, and valuation headroom large enough for a convex payoff, often five times or more. Passing earns a place, not a size.

    Part 5 · Torque: leverage on regime forces Exhibit P5-02 · Position Size Must Be Earned

    Related Torque Regime force Headroom Position sizing Conviction

  31. A predefined threshold that forces review or action before denial, emotion, or information overload can take over.

    Part 5 · Tripwires as position-management gates Exhibit L3 · Govern the Thesis

    Related Momentum filter CIS Agentic verification Fragility

Scoring

The two-score execution kernel and its cadence.

Part 6 · 27 terms

  1. The FIS reading of seventy: at or above it the portfolio holds, below it repair begins, with the attribution naming the fix. CIS reads the same four-band register, but there seventy is only the floor of the Strong band, a boundary rather than a trigger.

    Part 6 · Reading the number Exhibit P6-02 · FIS Starts at 100

    Related Score band FIS CIS Attribution

  2. The structural class a position belongs to, which selects the lens CIS scores it through. It changes how the rubric is applied, never what the final number is floored at.

    Part 6 · Archetype awareness Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related CIS TAM

  3. The itemized account of which rule cost how many points. It is what makes a construction score actionable, because the fix is named alongside the deduction.

    Part 6 · The five penalty buckets Exhibit P6-02 · FIS Starts at 100

    Related FIS Subtractive scoring Dead capital

  4. A sub-score inside Convexity and Optionality that prices identifiable, dated reasons for a re-rating. Each catalyst earns points from its impact, probability, independence, evidence confidence, and time decay, so several versions of the same catalyst do not count twice.

    Part 6 · The four CIS components Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related Convexity and Optionality (C) Headroom Confidence

  5. Convexity Integrity Score: a 0 to 100 score rating one position at a time on convexity and optionality, risk and fragility, macro alignment, and execution and sentiment.

    Part 6 · The formal scoring definition Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related Convexity Fragility Momentum filter Macro thesis

  6. How much the evidence behind a score can support, derived by the engine from the quality of each source rather than asserted by hand. It sets how far a single update is allowed to move the score.

    Part 6 · Confidence is derived, not asserted

    Related Delta clamp CIS

  7. All CIS sub-scores are continuous values rather than bucketed tiers: a position scores 78.3, not 75 or 80. Continuity preserves the small week-over-week movement that longitudinal tracking exists to see.

    Part 6 · Mechanics: floats, not tiers

    Related CIS Delta clamp Score decay

  8. The heaviest CIS component at forty percent, because asymmetric upside is the objective. It scores TAM headroom, the optionality surface, catalyst density, and scarcity, each capped, summing to a 0 to 100 component score.

    Part 6 · The four CIS components Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related CIS Headroom Catalyst density Optionality Convexity

  9. The failure CIS cannot see because it scores one position at a time: several high-scoring positions that move together under regime stress. Average correlation above 0.7 is flagged as a diagnostic; any penalty routes through FIS and governance, never through CIS.

    Part 6 · How implementations quietly degrade Exhibit P6-05 · Failure Rarely Arrives All at Once

    Related FIS Regime throttle Correlation instability CIS

  10. Capital held without a documented thesis or on a score nobody has refreshed. It is one of the five FIS penalty buckets, and it scales with position size.

    Part 6 · The five penalty buckets Exhibit P6-02 · FIS Starts at 100

    Related FIS Attribution

  11. The record of what changed, why, and what would reverse it, written as the weekly loop closes. It is what makes the next week’s pass a measurement rather than a memory.

    Part 6 · The weekly workflow Exhibit P6-04 · The Weekly Evidence Loop

    Related FIS CIS

  12. A cap on how far a score may move in a single update, scaled by how good the underlying evidence is. It forces a large re-rating to be earned across successive updates rather than granted in one enthusiastic week.

    Part 6 · Delta clamping Exhibit P6-04 · The Weekly Evidence Loop

    Related CIS Confidence

  13. The lightest CIS component at ten percent: momentum, relative strength, and market acceptance. It carries the least weight because execution confirms quality and never dominates it.

    Part 6 · The four CIS components Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related CIS Momentum filter 52-week high Breadth

  14. Framework Integrity Score: a 0 to 100 portfolio-construction score that starts the assembled portfolio at 100 and deducts a named penalty for each rule violation, so every lost point is attributable and repairable.

    Part 6 · The subtractive construction score Exhibit P6-02 · FIS Starts at 100

    Related CIS Posture Tax wrapper

  15. How much larger the addressable market is than the company, the first and largest sub-score inside Convexity and Optionality. It is scored on a logarithmic curve capped at thirty times, so the first multiple of headroom counts for far more than the twentieth.

    Part 6 · The four CIS components Exhibit P6-01 · CIS Measures the Position, Not the Portfolio

    Related TAM Convexity and Optionality (C) Torque eligibility Catalyst density

  16. The four events that interrupt the weekly cadence rather than wait for it: a position moving more than five percent in one day, material news, an earnings announcement, or a tripwire condition met. Between triggers, frequency limits keep activity from passing for diligence.

    Part 6 · Intra-week triggers Exhibit P6-04 · The Weekly Evidence Loop

    Related Weekly loop Tripwire Earnings proximity Restraint principle

  17. The CIS component, weighted twenty-five percent, that measures fit to the current regime rather than a forecast: regime sensitivity, carry direction, and policy alignment against the Part 2 thesis. A macro read may tilt a score; it is bounded so it can never determine one.

  18. The five named deductions FIS can take from one hundred: allocation, governance, dead capital, concentration, and complexity, each with its own cap. Because the caps sum to eighty, FIS can never fall below twenty, and every point lost names the rule that cost it.

  19. The gap between the portfolio’s actual posture mix and its target, which the market can open without a single trade. It is reported as a diagnostic alongside the score rather than billed as a penalty.

  20. The ten-point signal on score movement. A CIS rise of ten points flags the position for resizing toward its larger target, a fall of ten flags a downsize, and either is paced over two to four weeks. Neither changes posture, which Part 5 governs, and neither alone forces an exit.

  21. Discipline includes doing nothing. A CIS or FIS change under five points is monitored, a position inside its band is not resized, and a week in which every check passed and nothing moved is the system working, not the system idle.
